I. $U=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$

II. $V=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $W=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of the given sets as 
$\{{u}_{1},{u}_{2}\},$ 
$\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ and 
$\{{w}_{1},{w}_{2}\},$ respectively. 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.$

- ${v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=0,\,{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{3}=0,\,{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{3}=0.$

- ${w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=-3+0-2+2=-3\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $U$ is not an orthogonal set.

- For the set $V,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=4-4=0 & ✓ \\ {v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=2+0-4+2=0 & ✓ \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=0+6-4-2=0 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $V$ is orthogonal.

- For the set $W,$ notice that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=2+2+4=8\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $W$ is not an orthogonal set.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "$V$ only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c1c41282-b496-53fd-b601-ecca0a4b4a0c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-c1c41282-b496-53fd-b601-ecca0a4b4a0c" :answer-field/id #uuid "c1c41282-b496-53fd-b601-ecca0a4b4a0c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-b440af9e-0d7a-5e18-bcec-b34eee928e3f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c833776b-5d21-59ee-8ccb-29989a9b9e8a" "answer-7d1dfe6a-46a2-5b7b-b9a2-2e4f0b6a6290" "answer-2e486175-d93e-59a1-beee-b5e17fb3fe9f" "answer-b440af9e-0d7a-5e18-bcec-b34eee928e3f" "answer-99a6a3de-f047-5ffa-a17f-a1fea25b4278"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c833776b-5d21-59ee-8ccb-29989a9b9e8a" :answer/id #uuid "c833776b-5d21-59ee-8ccb-29989a9b9e8a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$U$ and $W$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7d1dfe6a-46a2-5b7b-b9a2-2e4f0b6a6290" :answer/id #uuid "7d1dfe6a-46a2-5b7b-b9a2-2e4f0b6a6290" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$U$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2e486175-d93e-59a1-beee-b5e17fb3fe9f" :answer/id #uuid "2e486175-d93e-59a1-beee-b5e17fb3fe9f" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$V$ and $W$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b440af9e-0d7a-5e18-bcec-b34eee928e3f" :answer/id #uuid "b440af9e-0d7a-5e18-bcec-b34eee928e3f" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$V$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-99a6a3de-f047-5ffa-a17f-a1fea25b4278" :answer/id #uuid "99a6a3de-f047-5ffa-a17f-a1fea25b4278" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$W$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-9cc85c8f-2fc1-51b5-90b3-b4c40aaa9ac5" :question/id #uuid "9cc85c8f-2fc1-51b5-90b3-b4c40aaa9ac5" :question/math-academy-id "q-40288" :question/problem "Which of the following sets are orthogonal?

I. $U=\{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}15 \\ -20\end{aligned}]\}$

II. $V=\{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $W=\{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\}$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of the given sets as 
$\{{u}_{1},{u}_{2},{u}_{3}\},$ 
$\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\},$ and 
$\{{w}_{1},{w}_{2},{w}_{3}\},$ respectively. 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0,\,{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=0,\,{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3}=0.$

- ${v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=0.$

- ${w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0,\,{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{3}=0,\,{w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{3}=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- The set $U$ cannot be orthogonal since it contains  $3$ vectors from ${R}^{2}$ (in which we can have an orthogonal set with at most 2 non-zero vectors). Therefore, $U$ is not an orthogonal set.

- For the set $V,$ notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=0+10=10\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $V$ is not an orthogonal set.

- For the set $W,$ notice that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=12+3-1=14\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $W$ is not an orthogonal set.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "None of the listed"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-88d26e7d-7cf7-53de-a739-9d6548330c1e"] :question/problem "Which of the following sets are orthonormal?

I. $U=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\}$

II. $V=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -1 \\ -9\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $W=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ -\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]\}$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of the given sets as 
$\{{u}_{1},{u}_{2}\},$ 
$\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ and 
$\{{w}_{1},{w}_{2}\},$ respectively. 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthonormal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}=1 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

- $\{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=0 \\ {v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{3}=0 \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}=1 \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}=1 \\ {v}_{3}\cdot {v}_{3}=1.\end{aligned}$

- ${w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1}=1 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}=0 & ✓ \\ {u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1 & ✓ \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $U$ is orthonormal.

- For the set $V,$ notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=0+12+6=18\ne 1 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $V$ is not an orthonormal set.

- For the set $W,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ -\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]=\frac{12}{25}-\frac{12}{25}=0 & ✓ \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]=\frac{16}{25}+\frac{9}{25}=1 & ✓ \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ -\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ -\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]=\frac{9}{25}+\frac{16}{25}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, $W$ is an orthonormal set.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "$U$ and $W$ only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e09f4fd9-728c-5fad-860e-671199dd6464"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e09f4fd9-728c-5fad-860e-671199dd6464" :answer-field/id #uuid "e09f4fd9-728c-5fad-860e-671199dd6464" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-a054e702-a15a-5f24-9814-706df32db073" :answer-field/choices ["answer-2454dddf-8213-5a02-af2b-3a48c11de7c7" "answer-a054e702-a15a-5f24-9814-706df32db073" "answer-1973b4e5-3021-5f0e-84fb-21f789bd603c" "answer-a2e77911-f7b1-5d0a-99ba-fbc6c3057279" "answer-625d32a2-e015-5a3c-a155-566556b8fd99"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2454dddf-8213-5a02-af2b-3a48c11de7c7" :answer/id #uuid "2454dddf-8213-5a02-af2b-3a48c11de7c7" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$U$ and $V$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a054e702-a15a-5f24-9814-706df32db073" :answer/id #uuid "a054e702-a15a-5f24-9814-706df32db073" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$U$ and $W$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1973b4e5-3021-5f0e-84fb-21f789bd603c" :answer/id #uuid "1973b4e5-3021-5f0e-84fb-21f789bd603c" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$U$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a2e77911-f7b1-5d0a-99ba-fbc6c3057279" :answer/id #uuid "a2e77911-f7b1-5d0a-99ba-fbc6c3057279" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$V$ and $W$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-625d32a2-e015-5a3c-a155-566556b8fd99" :answer/id #uuid "625d32a2-e015-5a3c-a155-566556b8fd99" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$W$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186351223 :question/problem "Which of the following sets are orthonormal?

I. $U=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\}$

II. $V=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $W=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]\}$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of the given sets as 
$\{{u}_{1},{u}_{2},{u}_{3}\},$ 
$\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\},$ and 
$\{{w}_{1},{w}_{2}\},$ respectively. 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthonormal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- $\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0 \\ {u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}=1 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}=1 \\ {u}_{3}\cdot {u}_{3}=1.\end{aligned}$

- ${v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}=1 \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

- $\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0 \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{3}=0 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1}=1 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2}=1 \\ {w}_{3}\cdot {w}_{3}=1.\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=1+25+4=30\ne 1 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $U$ is not an orthonormal set.

- For the set $V,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=-\frac{6}{13}+\frac{6}{13}=0 & ✓ \\ {v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{4}{13}+\frac{9}{13}=1 & ✓ \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{9}{13}+\frac{4}{13}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $V$ is orthonormal.

- For the set $W,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{18}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}=0 & ✓ \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{4}{6}+\frac{1}{6}=1 & ✓ \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $W$ is orthonormal.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "$V$ and $W$ only"." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186370894 :question/problem "Consider the orthogonal set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $x=[{x}_{1},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}]^{T},$ extend the set so that it forms an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What is the value of $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}?$

$$
U=\{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]\}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $U$ as ${u}_{1},\,{u}_{2}.$ To extend the given set to an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{3}$, we need to find a third vector $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]$ such that

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}5{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}+7{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to its row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 3 & -4 & 7 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{5}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{26}{5} & \frac{38}{5} & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=\frac{19}{13}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}5{x}_{1} & ={x}_{3}-2(\frac{19}{13}{x}_{3}) \\ 5{x}_{1} & =-\frac{25}{13}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{1} & =-\frac{5}{13}{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{13}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{19}{13}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=13$ we obtain the vector 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 19 \\ 13\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{3}$ is

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 7\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 19 \\ 13\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Finally, $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}=-\frac{5}{19}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-93aa26c6-5456-5313-9c30-05baafe99b46" :question/id #uuid "93aa26c6-5456-5313-9c30-05baafe99b46" :question/math-academy-id "q-81112" :question/problem "Consider the orthogonal set $U$ below. Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to row echelon form, as follows:

$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-\frac{3}{10}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -3 \\ 10\end{aligned}].

Therefore, an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{3}$ is

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -3 \\ 10\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Finally, $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}=\frac{-6}{-3}=2.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ec92482d-c477-5d24-9a25-7a7af7728403"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ec92482d-c477-5d24-9a25-7a7af7728403" :answer-field/id #uuid "ec92482d-c477-5d24-9a25-7a7af7728403" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-44ed5e4f-8fa9-5c51-90b0-836168dfa8a9" :answer-field/choices ["answer-342bd711-7b57-5e5b-b53c-c41f6cf6ed52" "answer-44ed5e4f-8fa9-5c51-90b0-836168dfa8a9" "answer-c083b72f-3913-5a9b-bb4b-2b33c44b8374" "answer-15b18abf-20d4-5b53-b9f6-8b33f580740b" "answer-8e2ec803-638b-5ea2-ac14-1aac19cbda75"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-342bd711-7b57-5e5b-b53c-c41f6cf6ed52" :answer/id #uuid "342bd711-7b57-5e5b-b53c-c41f6cf6ed52" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-44ed5e4f-8fa9-5c51-90b0-836168dfa8a9" :answer/id #uuid "44ed5e4f-8fa9-5c51-90b0-836168dfa8a9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c083b72f-3913-5a9b-bb4b-2b33c44b8374" :answer/id #uuid "c083b72f-3913-5a9b-bb4b-2b33c44b8374" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-15b18abf-20d4-5b53-b9f6-8b33f580740b" :answer/id #uuid "15b18abf-20d4-5b53-b9f6-8b33f580740b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8e2ec803-638b-5ea2-ac14-1aac19cbda75" :answer/id #uuid "8e2ec803-638b-5ea2-ac14-1aac19cbda75" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-9e056f00-625c-54f9-921d-feb61293e496" :question/id #uuid "9e056f00-625c-54f9-921d-feb61293e496" :question/math-academy-id "q-83768" :question/problem "Consider the **orthonormal** set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $x=[{x}_{1},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}]^{T},$ extend the set so that it forms an **orthonormal** basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What is the value of $|{x}_{1}|+|{x}_{2}|+|{x}_{3}|?$

$$
U=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{21}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{21}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}}\end{aligned}]\}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $U$ as ${u}_{1},\,{u}_{2}.$ To extend the given set to an orthonormal basis of ${R}^{3}$, we need to find a third vector $x$ such that $‖x‖=1,$ and

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{3}=0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{21}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{21}}{x}_{2}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}}{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{21}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{21}} & -\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}} & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\sqrt{6}\cdot {R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=\sqrt{21}\cdot {R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}+2(-2{x}_{3})+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=3{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{3} \\ -2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we obtain the vector 
$x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Now, we need to normalize $x.$ Notice that $‖x‖=\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{14}.$ So, we normalize $x$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x}{‖x‖}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{14}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{14}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, an orthonormal basis of ${R}^{3}$ is

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{21}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{21}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{14}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{14}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Finally, $|{x}_{1}|+|{x}_{2}|+|{x}_{3}|=|\frac{3}{\sqrt{14}}|+|-\frac{2}{\sqrt{14}}|+|\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}|=\frac{6}{\sqrt{14}}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b6bbf667-f0ec-5670-9c25-934e766d8f09"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b6bbf667-f0ec-5670-9c25-934e766d8f09" :answer-field/id #uuid "b6bbf667-f0ec-5670-9c25-934e766d8f09" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-f906b041-d06e-5690-ab61-f1fbb040be89" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c2644191-8b0e-5649-af0f-0f586b12d76d" "answer-ab5a79ce-b244-589b-887d-eb3fa120294b" "answer-25cb96ba-aaf0-5535-b2bf-14442cb3e2c8" "answer-93c0c141-6245-5b52-b5d1-782e45040c14" "answer-f906b041-d06e-5690-ab61-f1fbb040be89"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c2644191-8b0e-5649-af0f-0f586b12d76d" :answer/id #uuid "c2644191-8b0e-5649-af0f-0f586b12d76d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{13}{\sqrt{14}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ab5a79ce-b244-589b-887d-eb3fa120294b" :answer/id #uuid "ab5a79ce-b244-589b-887d-eb3fa120294b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{\sqrt{14}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-25cb96ba-aaf0-5535-b2bf-14442cb3e2c8" :answer/id #uuid "25cb96ba-aaf0-5535-b2bf-14442cb3e2c8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{\sqrt{14}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-93c0c141-6245-5b52-b5d1-782e45040c14" :answer/id #uuid "93c0c141-6245-5b52-b5d1-782e45040c14" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{\sqrt{14}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f906b041-d06e-5690-ab61-f1fbb040be89" :answer/id #uuid "f906b041-d06e-5690-ab61-f1fbb040be89" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{6}{\sqrt{14}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186351226 :question/problem "Consider the **orthonormal** set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $x=[{x}_{1},\,{x}_{2}]^{T},$ extend the set so that it forms an **orthonormal** basis of ${R}^{2}.$ What is the value of $|{x}_{1}|+|{x}_{2}|?$

$$
U=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vector of $U$ as ${u}_{1}.$ To extend the given set to an orthonormal basis of ${R}^{2}$, we need to find a second vector $x$ such that $‖x‖=1,$ and

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot x=0\,⟹\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0.
$$

From the above equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we obtain the vector 
$x=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Now, we need to normalize $x.$ Notice that $‖x‖=\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{2}.$ So, we normalize $x$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x}{‖x‖}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, an orthonormal basis of ${R}^{2}$ is

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Finally, $|{x}_{1}|+|{x}_{2}|=|-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|+|\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135045 :tutorial/content "A set of vectors ${U}=\{ \mathbf{u}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{u}_p \}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is an **orthogonal set** if each pair of distinct vectors from the set is orthogonal.

For example, let's consider the following set:

![](images/9b/9b5afbbe850cb936b16b177e0a1b42bdd94df9bdc5dd3830aadc0de328a2b0d8.svg)

If we denote the vectors in our set ${W}$ as $\{ \mathbf{w}_1, \mathbf{w}_2, \mathbf{w}_3 \},$ we can check that ${W}$ is orthogonal by showing that 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0 \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{3}=0 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute each dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 2+1\cdot 1=0 & ✓ \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]=3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot (-4)+1\cdot 7=0 & ✓ \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]=(-1)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot (-4)+1\cdot 7=0 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So indeed, ${W}$ is an orthogonal set.

If an orthogonal set is also a basis, then we call it an **orthogonal basis**. Here, $W$ is an orthogonal basis of $\mathbb{R}^3,$ because it contains three linearly independent (you can check this) orthogonal vectors." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133990 :activity/expected-seconds 1140.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.$

- ${v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=0,\,{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{3}=0,\,{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{3}=0.$

- ${w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=-3+0-2+2=-3\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $U$ is not an orthogonal set.

- For the set $V,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=4-4=0 & ✓ \\ {v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=2+0-4+2=0 & ✓ \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=0+6-4-2=0 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $V$ is orthogonal.

- For the set $W,$ notice that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=2+2+4=8\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $W$ is not an orthogonal set.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "$V$ only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c1c41282-b496-53fd-b601-ecca0a4b4a0c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-c1c41282-b496-53fd-b601-ecca0a4b4a0c" :answer-field/id #uuid "c1c41282-b496-53fd-b601-ecca0a4b4a0c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-b440af9e-0d7a-5e18-bcec-b34eee928e3f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c833776b-5d21-59ee-8ccb-29989a9b9e8a" "answer-7d1dfe6a-46a2-5b7b-b9a2-2e4f0b6a6290" "answer-2e486175-d93e-59a1-beee-b5e17fb3fe9f" "answer-b440af9e-0d7a-5e18-bcec-b34eee928e3f" "answer-99a6a3de-f047-5ffa-a17f-a1fea25b4278"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c833776b-5d21-59ee-8ccb-29989a9b9e8a" :answer/id #uuid "c833776b-5d21-59ee-8ccb-29989a9b9e8a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$U$ and $W$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7d1dfe6a-46a2-5b7b-b9a2-2e4f0b6a6290" :answer/id #uuid "7d1dfe6a-46a2-5b7b-b9a2-2e4f0b6a6290" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$U$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2e486175-d93e-59a1-beee-b5e17fb3fe9f" :answer/id #uuid "2e486175-d93e-59a1-beee-b5e17fb3fe9f" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$V$ and $W$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b440af9e-0d7a-5e18-bcec-b34eee928e3f" :answer/id #uuid "b440af9e-0d7a-5e18-bcec-b34eee928e3f" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$V$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-99a6a3de-f047-5ffa-a17f-a1fea25b4278" :answer/id #uuid "99a6a3de-f047-5ffa-a17f-a1fea25b4278" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$W$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-9cc85c8f-2fc1-51b5-90b3-b4c40aaa9ac5" :question/id #uuid "9cc85c8f-2fc1-51b5-90b3-b4c40aaa9ac5" :question/math-academy-id "q-40288" :question/problem "Which of the following sets are orthogonal?

:question/problem "Which of the following sets are orthonormal?

III. $W=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ -\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]\}$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of the given sets as 
$\{{u}_{1},{u}_{2}\},$ 
$\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ and 
$\{{w}_{1},{w}_{2}\},$ respectively. 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthonormal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}=1 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

- $\{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=0 \\ {v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{3}=0 \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}=1 \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}=1 \\ {v}_{3}\cdot {v}_{3}=1.\end{aligned}$

- ${w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1}=1 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}=0 & ✓ \\ {u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1 & ✓ \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $U$ is orthonormal.

- For the set $V,$ notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=0+12+6=18\ne 1 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $V$ is not an orthonormal set.

- For the set $W,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ -\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]=\frac{12}{25}-\frac{12}{25}=0 & ✓ \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]=\frac{16}{25}+\frac{9}{25}=1 & ✓ \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ -\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ -\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]=\frac{9}{25}+\frac{16}{25}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, $W$ is an orthonormal set.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "$U$ and $W$ only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e09f4fd9-728c-5fad-860e-671199dd6464"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e09f4fd9-728c-5fad-860e-671199dd6464" :answer-field/id #uuid "e09f4fd9-728c-5fad-860e-671199dd6464" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-a054e702-a15a-5f24-9814-706df32db073" :answer-field/choices ["answer-2454dddf-8213-5a02-af2b-3a48c11de7c7" "answer-a054e702-a15a-5f24-9814-706df32db073" "answer-1973b4e5-3021-5f0e-84fb-21f789bd603c" "answer-a2e77911-f7b1-5d0a-99ba-fbc6c3057279" "answer-625d32a2-e015-5a3c-a155-566556b8fd99"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2454dddf-8213-5a02-af2b-3a48c11de7c7" :answer/id #uuid "2454dddf-8213-5a02-af2b-3a48c11de7c7" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$U$ and $V$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a054e702-a15a-5f24-9814-706df32db073" :answer/id #uuid "a054e702-a15a-5f24-9814-706df32db073" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$U$ and $W$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1973b4e5-3021-5f0e-84fb-21f789bd603c" :answer/id #uuid "1973b4e5-3021-5f0e-84fb-21f789bd603c" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$U$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a2e77911-f7b1-5d0a-99ba-fbc6c3057279" :answer/id #uuid "a2e77911-f7b1-5d0a-99ba-fbc6c3057279" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$V$ and $W$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-625d32a2-e015-5a3c-a155-566556b8fd99" :answer/id #uuid "625d32a2-e015-5a3c-a155-566556b8fd99" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$W$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186351223 :question/problem "Which of the following sets are orthonormal?

II. $V=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $W=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]\}$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of the given sets as 
$\{{u}_{1},{u}_{2},{u}_{3}\},$ 
$\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\},$ and 
$\{{w}_{1},{w}_{2}\},$ respectively. 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthonormal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- $\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0 \\ {u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}=1 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}=1 \\ {u}_{3}\cdot {u}_{3}=1.\end{aligned}$

- ${v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}=1 \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

- $\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0 \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{3}=0 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1}=1 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2}=1 \\ {w}_{3}\cdot {w}_{3}=1.\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=1+25+4=30\ne 1 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $U$ is not an orthonormal set.

- For the set $V,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=-\frac{6}{13}+\frac{6}{13}=0 & ✓ \\ {v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{4}{13}+\frac{9}{13}=1 & ✓ \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{9}{13}+\frac{4}{13}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $V$ is orthonormal.

- For the set $W,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{18}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}=0 & ✓ \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{4}{6}+\frac{1}{6}=1 & ✓ \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $W$ is orthonormal.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "$V$ and $W$ only"." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186370894 :question/problem "Consider the orthogonal set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $x=[{x}_{1},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}]^{T},$ extend the set so that it forms an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What is the value of $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}?$

$$
U=\{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]\}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $U$ as ${u}_{1},\,{u}_{2}.$ To extend the given set to an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{3}$, we need to find a third vector $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]$ such that

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}5{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}+7{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to its row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 3 & -4 & 7 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{5}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{26}{5} & \frac{38}{5} & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=\frac{19}{13}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}5{x}_{1} & ={x}_{3}-2(\frac{19}{13}{x}_{3}) \\ 5{x}_{1} & =-\frac{25}{13}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{1} & =-\frac{5}{13}{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{13}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{19}{13}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.

$$

Therefore, an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{3}$ is

$$

Finally, $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}=-\frac{5}{19}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-93aa26c6-5456-5313-9c30-05baafe99b46" :question/id #uuid "93aa26c6-5456-5313-9c30-05baafe99b46" :question/math-academy-id "q-81112" :question/problem "Consider the orthogonal set $U$ below. In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-\frac{3}{10}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

By adding a new vector $x=[{x}_{1},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}]^{T},$ extend the set so that it forms an **orthonormal** basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What is the value of $|{x}_{1}|+|{x}_{2}|+|{x}_{3}|?$

$$
U=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{21}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{21}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}}\end{aligned}]\}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $U$ as ${u}_{1},\,{u}_{2}.$ To extend the given set to an orthonormal basis of ${R}^{3}$, we need to find a third vector $x$ such that $‖x‖=1,$ and

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{3}=0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{21}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{21}}{x}_{2}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}}{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{21}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{21}} & -\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}} & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\sqrt{6}\cdot {R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=\sqrt{21}\cdot {R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}+2(-2{x}_{3})+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=3{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{3} \\ -2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we obtain the vector 
$x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Now, we need to normalize $x.$ Notice that $‖x‖=\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{14}.$ So, we normalize $x$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x}{‖x‖}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{14}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{14}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, an orthonormal basis of ${R}^{3}$ is

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{21}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{21}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{14}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{14}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Finally, $|{x}_{1}|+|{x}_{2}|+|{x}_{3}|=|\frac{3}{\sqrt{14}}|+|-\frac{2}{\sqrt{14}}|+|\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}|=\frac{6}{\sqrt{14}}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b6bbf667-f0ec-5670-9c25-934e766d8f09"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b6bbf667-f0ec-5670-9c25-934e766d8f09" :answer-field/id #uuid "b6bbf667-f0ec-5670-9c25-934e766d8f09" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-f906b041-d06e-5690-ab61-f1fbb040be89" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c2644191-8b0e-5649-af0f-0f586b12d76d" "answer-ab5a79ce-b244-589b-887d-eb3fa120294b" "answer-25cb96ba-aaf0-5535-b2bf-14442cb3e2c8" "answer-93c0c141-6245-5b52-b5d1-782e45040c14" "answer-f906b041-d06e-5690-ab61-f1fbb040be89"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c2644191-8b0e-5649-af0f-0f586b12d76d" :answer/id #uuid "c2644191-8b0e-5649-af0f-0f586b12d76d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{13}{\sqrt{14}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ab5a79ce-b244-589b-887d-eb3fa120294b" :answer/id #uuid "ab5a79ce-b244-589b-887d-eb3fa120294b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{\sqrt{14}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-25cb96ba-aaf0-5535-b2bf-14442cb3e2c8" :answer/id #uuid "25cb96ba-aaf0-5535-b2bf-14442cb3e2c8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{\sqrt{14}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-93c0c141-6245-5b52-b5d1-782e45040c14" :answer/id #uuid "93c0c141-6245-5b52-b5d1-782e45040c14" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{\sqrt{14}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f906b041-d06e-5690-ab61-f1fbb040be89" :answer/id #uuid "f906b041-d06e-5690-ab61-f1fbb040be89" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{6}{\sqrt{14}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186351226 :question/problem "Consider the **orthonormal** set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $x=[{x}_{1},\,{x}_{2}]^{T},$ extend the set so that it forms an **orthonormal** basis of ${R}^{2}.$ What is the value of $|{x}_{1}|+|{x}_{2}|?$

$$
U=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vector of $U$ as ${u}_{1}.$ To extend the given set to an orthonormal basis of ${R}^{2}$, we need to find a second vector $x$ such that $‖x‖=1,$ and

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot x=0\,⟹\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0.
$$

From the above equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we obtain the vector 
$x=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Now, we need to normalize $x.$ Notice that $‖x‖=\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{2}.$ So, we normalize $x$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x}{‖x‖}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, an orthonormal basis of ${R}^{2}$ is

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Finally, $|{x}_{1}|+|{x}_{2}|=|-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|+|\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135045 :tutorial/content "A set of vectors ${U}=\{ \mathbf{u}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{u}_p \}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is an **orthogonal set** if each pair of distinct vectors from the set is orthogonal.

For example, let's consider the following set:

![](images/9b/9b5afbbe850cb936b16b177e0a1b42bdd94df9bdc5dd3830aadc0de328a2b0d8.svg)

If we denote the vectors in our set ${W}$ as $\{ \mathbf{w}_1, \mathbf{w}_2, \mathbf{w}_3 \},$ we can check that ${W}$ is orthogonal by showing that 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0 \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{3}=0 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute each dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 2+1\cdot 1=0 & ✓ \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]=3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot (-4)+1\cdot 7=0 & ✓ \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]=(-1)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot (-4)+1\cdot 7=0 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So indeed, ${W}$ is an orthogonal set.

If an orthogonal set is also a basis, then we call it an **orthogonal basis**. Here, $W$ is an orthogonal basis of $\mathbb{R}^3,$ because it contains three linearly independent (you can check this) orthogonal vectors." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133990 :activity/expected-seconds 1140.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186133658 :question/problem "Determine whether the following set is orthogonal:
![](images/5b/5b51a8ec772d084cb7c4ac85b6e6ac71e9d128242a6553348e7ea9ec57e8c3dc.svg)"] [17592186133658 :question/worked-solution "If we denote the vectors in our set ${X}$ as $\{ \mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \mathbf{x}_3 \},$ we can check that ${X}$ is orthogonal by showing that 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.$

- ${v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=0,\,{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{3}=0,\,{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{3}=0.$

- ${w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=-3+0-2+2=-3\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $U$ is not an orthogonal set.

- For the set $V,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=4-4=0 & ✓ \\ {v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=2+0-4+2=0 & ✓ \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=0+6-4-2=0 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $V$ is orthogonal.

- For the set $W,$ notice that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=2+2+4=8\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $W$ is not an orthogonal set.

["question-bccef2e2-efdc-5751-b184-d287795e3e5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-82399"] ["question-bccef2e2-efdc-5751-b184-d287795e3e5f" :question/problem "Which of the following sets are orthonormal?

$\{{u}_{1},{u}_{2}\},$ 
$\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ and 
$\{{w}_{1},{w}_{2}\},$ respectively. 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthonormal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}=1 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

- $\{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=0 \\ {v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{3}=0 \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}=1 \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}=1 \\ {v}_{3}\cdot {v}_{3}=1.\end{aligned}$

- ${w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1}=1 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}=0 & ✓ \\ {u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1 & ✓ \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $U$ is orthonormal.

- For the set $V,$ notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=0+12+6=18\ne 1 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $V$ is not an orthonormal set.

$$

$$

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{21}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{21}} & -\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}} & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\sqrt{6}\cdot {R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=\sqrt{21}\cdot {R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{3} \\ -2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

$x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Now, we need to normalize $x.$ Notice that $‖x‖=\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{14}.$ So, we normalize $x$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x}{‖x‖}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{14}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{14}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, an orthonormal basis of ${R}^{3}$ is

$$

The set $W$ is orthonormal if the following conditions hold:

![](images/1a/1a2b4f5d6fb8842115feb6e6f12ac70399768c94006966838c3817eabd85e7fb.png)

With that in mind, let's examine our set:

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}=0 & ✓ \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1 & ✓ \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=16+16=32\ne 1 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

We see that $\mathbf w_1$ and $\mathbf w_2$ are orthogonal, and $\mathbf w_1$ is a unit vector, but $\mathbf w_2$ is *not* a unit vector.

Therefore, ${W}$ is *not* an orthonormal set."} {:db/id 17592186048849} {:db/id 17592186134215 :question/id #uuid "89970297-1b2c-5ba8-b18f-ccd95df5c317" :question/math-academy-id "q-39398"} {:db/id The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthonormal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- ${\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0 \\ {u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}=1 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}=1 \\ {u}_{3}\cdot {u}_{3}=1.\end{aligned}$

- ${v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}=1 \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

- ${\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0 \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{3}=0 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1}=1 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2}=1 \\ {w}_{3}\cdot {w}_{3}=1.\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=1+25+4=30\ne 1 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $U$ is not an orthonormal set.

- For the set $V,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=-\frac{6}{13}+\frac{6}{13}=0 & ✓ \\ {v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{4}{13}+\frac{9}{13}=1 & ✓ \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{9}{13}+\frac{4}{13}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $V$ is orthonormal.

- For the set $W,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{18}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}=0 & ✓ \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{4}{6}+\frac{1}{6}=1 & ✓ \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $W$ is orthonormal.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "$V$ and $W$ only"."} {:db/id 17592186351423 :question/id #uuid "2c1e164f-769d-52d4-a09c-f8474e7b2368" :question/math-academy-id "q-82401"} {:db/id $$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.

$$
\frac{x}{‖x‖}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]}.
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute each dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=2\cdot (-1)+0\cdot 0+1\cdot 2=0 & ✓ \\ {x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=2\cdot 1+0\cdot (-2)+1\cdot 0=2\ne 0 & \times  \\ {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=(-1)\cdot 1+0\cdot (-2)+2\cdot 0=-1\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So ${X}$ is *not* an orthogonal set."} {:db/id 17592186134222 :question/id #uuid "9159a670-da1f-50b2-8f30-7247d3a89a7e" :question/math-academy-id "q-39490"} {:db/id 17592186134286 :question/id #uuid :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134663 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135045 :tutorial/content "A set of vectors ${U}=\{ \mathbf{u}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{u}_p \}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is an **orthogonal set** if each pair of distinct vectors from the set is orthogonal.

For example, let's consider the following set:

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

If we denote the vectors in our set ${W}$ as $\{ \mathbf{w}_1, \mathbf{w}_2, \mathbf{w}_3 \},$ we can check that ${W}$ is orthogonal by showing that 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0 \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{3}=0 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute each dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 2+1\cdot 1=0 & ✓ \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]=3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot (-4)+1\cdot 7=0 & ✓ \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]=(-1)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot (-4)+1\cdot 7=0 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So indeed, ${W}$ is an orthogonal set.

If an orthogonal set is also a basis, then we call it an **orthogonal basis**. Here, $W$ is an orthogonal basis of $\mathbb{R}^3,$ because it contains three linearly independent (you can check this) orthogonal vectors." :tutorial/id #uuid "dd93c4b2-6ec7-5a9c-a669-7979210393dd" :tutorial/content "A set of vectors ${U}=\{ \mathbf{u}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{u}_p \}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is an **orthogonal set** if each pair of distinct vectors from the set is orthogonal.

For example, let's consider the following set:

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

If we denote the vectors in our set ${W}$ as $\{ \mathbf{w}_1, \mathbf{w}_2, \mathbf{w}_3 \},$ we can check that ${W}$ is orthogonal by showing that 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0 \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{3}=0 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute each dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 2+1\cdot 1=0 & ✓ \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]=3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot (-4)+1\cdot 7=0 & ✓ \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]=(-1)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot (-4)+1\cdot 7=0 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So indeed, ${W}$ is an orthogonal set.

If an orthogonal set is also a basis, then we call it an **orthogonal basis**. Here, $W$ is an orthogonal basis of $\mathbb{R}^3,$ because it contains three linearly independent (you can check this) orthogonal vectors." :tutorial/id #uuid "dd93c4b2-6ec7-5a9c-a669-7979210393dd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3618 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "86221c16-9568-5f86-9e0e-496ed4975fdb" :step/math-academy-id 20224 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134772}} {:db/id 17592186135045 :tutorial/content "A set of vectors ${U}=\{ \mathbf{u}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{u}_p \}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is an **orthogonal set** if each pair of distinct vectors from the set is orthogonal.

[17592186046658 1005 17592186046975 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1007 "Mathematics for Machine Learning" 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.
This course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.
On completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.
Students then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.
As part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.
Students will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.
The course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.
A solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.
Students also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.
Students work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.
On the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.
Students extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.
